title: Just In Time
author: Terry Yu
summary: Terry Yu proposes a new concept -- 'nom,' the human in the act of learning -- and uses it to analyze what he calls schools' 'impoverished time grammar.' The piece argues that schools operate with only two tenses of learning: the past (what has been taught and assessed) and the future (what will be taught and tested). What is missing is a rich vocabulary and set of practices for the present -- for the learner in the act of encountering something new, being confused, holding a question without a quick resolution, and sitting with productive uncertainty. Yu observes that the architecture of the traditional school day is designed to minimize the time spent in productive confusion, whereas most genuine learning happens precisely in that uncomfortable state. The nom concept is both a diagnostic (here is what schools systematically neglect) and a design brief (here is what schools could build more of: structured time for productive confusion, explicit practices for the learner in the act of encountering the hard thing).
points: * The 'nom' concept names the person in the specific act of learning -- not the learner in general but the human in the moment of encounter with something not yet understood -- a subject that schools have no rich vocabulary for. * Schools operate with an impoverished time grammar: past tense (what has been taught) and future tense (what will be tested) dominate, while the present tense of learning -- the nom in productive confusion -- is systematically minimized. * The traditional school day is architecturally designed to minimize time in productive confusion, whereas most genuine learning happens precisely in that uncomfortable in-between state. * The vocabulary gap is a design gap: without a word for the learner in the act, schools have no framework for designing time, space, or pedagogical practices around that person's specific experience and needs. * The nom concept is simultaneously diagnostic (schools neglect the present tense of learning) and prescriptive (design practices for the learner in the moment of productive encounter with the hard thing).
quotes: I want to propose a word: nom. The nom is you, right now, in the act of learning something you don't yet understand. Not you as a student, which is a role. Not you as a learner, which is a general disposition. The nom is you in the specific moment of encounter -- confused, curious, somewhere between not-knowing and knowing.

Schools have a very rich grammar for the past and the future of learning. They can describe what has been taught, what has been assessed, what has been retained. They can describe what will be taught, what will be tested, what is expected. They have almost no grammar for the present -- for the nom, in the act, right now.

The entire architecture of the school day is designed, in effect, to minimize time in productive confusion. Transitions, schedules, lessons that end at the bell whether the thinking is done or not -- these are not neutral choices. They are choices about whose experience matters and when.

The nom is the most important person in education. She is the reason any of it exists. And we have no word for her, which means we have no framework for designing around her experience, and which means we consistently fail to do so.

A school that took the nom seriously would look different. It would have scheduled time for sitting with a hard question without a required outcome. It would treat productive confusion as evidence of learning, not as a problem to solve with a clearer explanation. It would be organized around the experience of the person in the moment of encounter.
